pr_title: unprivileged DDI mounts + dynamic userns range allocation via IPC
pr_body:
This adds two concepts: a new, small daemon systemd-mntfsd, which allows mounting DDIs via IPC calls. It will return fsmount() fds, that the client can then attach to any directory it wants to.

It also extends systemd-userdbd with a new varlink call for writing a userns mapping into a userns fd, similar in fashion to the "newuidmap" tool, but without involving SUID logic, and transiently.

This is currently work in process, and still full of glaring security holes. Specifically:

* ~~We need to lock down DDI mounting, i.e. #25608~~
* ~~Currently if the userns allocation is used, clients may gain persistency, though they should really not~~
* ~~we need some form of access control (polkit?) to the two IPC apis~~

Fixes: #30239

In terms of policy, we really need to tight things down (I understand it's WIP for now), so I'm thinking:

1) By default, no unprivileged process can ask for this
2) Add a config knob to enable unprivileged process to ask for signed DDIs (ie, with dm-verity signature verified by the kernel)

Current plan regarding the UID range persistency:

The attack scenario goes like this: an unpriv user allocates a userns range via our service. Then joins it, but does not enter any mount namespace and instead writes executable files to /tmp and /var/tmp with suid bit set from inside the userns. Thus, from the host it can later, persistently, reacquire access to the uid range via the suid vector.

Currently, our model of thinking how to close this specific gap:

write a bpf-lsm module that maintains a bpf map that keyed by a userns has an allowlist of fsmounts that access is allowed to. Then, restrict file system access so that a process may only access files on mounts that are either owned by its own userns or are allowlisted by the mentioned bpf map. Then, when a process acquires a userns via userdbd it would get it set up so that it can basically access nothing, and then when it talks to mntfsd we'd add an entry to the map that allowlists the fsmounts we just created.

Essentially this gives us a "focussed" userns: no access to anything but what we later grant it access to.

When using LSMs it is common to separate privileges, so that for example writing files is allowed, but mounting is not. But this escalates the former into the latter automatically. Policy writers by now are well aware that allowing to write arbitrary unit files in /etc/systemd/system/ and friends means being able to do anything on a system - but this is not really true for other directories such as container images directories. An image downloading service that is allowed to write images to /var/lib/machines is now implicitly allowed to mount them too.
This option is certainly useful to have, but I think it would be much better to have a command line flag or environment variable that has to be enabled for this criteria to be used.

> If the disk image contains a Verity enabled disk image, along with a signature partition with a key in the kernel keyring the disk image is considered trusted.

This bit from the manpage is not quite accurate, as the certificates in /etc/ are also used as a fallback. Incidentally, for this purpose the fallback should be opt-in, and used only if explicitly enabled in the service cmdline or via an env var.

So I have reworked this now a bit. With this we'll now query polkit for any mount and for all clients (including for root!), however we ask for different actions to be authorized. Specifically:

1. There are two sets of actions now: if we want to mount a DDI into the host userns, or into some private userns. (Assumption is that DDIs mounted into the host requires stronger authorization)

2. We now ask for a "low-priv" action first, and then mount with a strict image policy (i.e verity is required). If that doesn't work, we ask for a "high-priv" action next, and if that is accepted we'll mount with a weak iage policy (i.e. verity is not required).

There's one more tweak to the rule though: if the image is located below /usr/ (i.e already subject to package manager's protection/or OS-level verity) we also allow mounting it with the "low-priv" polkit action but the "weak" image policy.

Thus: if an image is in the trusted dir or not doesn't mean you'll bypass PK checks anymore. it just changes how much you get after PK authorization.

There is very little consistent difference between `/usr` and `/var`. It is certainly not true that `/usr` is "subject to package manager's protection/or OS-level verity", at least not in the general case. Maybe in some specific cases like image-based distros that don't allow local overrides. In fact, many distributions will allow unprivileged users to install arbitrary packages from the distro, which may contain many different files, including test files and whatnot. 

I think it'd be totally fine for a distro that *does have* those protections in place to put in a custom polkit rule, but the default should be to not make any assumptions about `/usr`.

I think the chain of trust for this should be rooted in hardware, and while the mok keyring is one way to do it, it's not the only one - if you build a kernel you can add to the trusted keyring, you can also self-enroll in firmware's db. In fact, I'm pretty sure in some cases like coco you don't want mok at all!
> > But the problem here is not even the keyring chain of trust, it's that "mere" writing privileges to a "special" directory give implicit access to much higher capabilities, which I am sure it's a footgun that we should not bake in.
> > Of course adding it optionally is perfectly fine compromise by me - so that one can choose to buy into this model if they want to, so thanks for implementing that, I'll re-review as soon as I can.
> 
> I didn't look at the latest version of the code, but looking just at the discussion here, I think @bluca is right.
> 
> There is very little consistent difference between `/usr` and `/var`. It is certainly not true that `/usr` is "subject to package manager's protection/or OS-level verity", at least not in the general case. Maybe in some specific cases like image-based distros that don't allow local overrides. In fact, many distributions will allow unprivileged users to install arbitrary packages from the distro, which may contain many different files, including test files and whatnot.
> 
> I think it'd be totally fine for a distro that _does have_ those protections in place to put in a custom polkit rule, but the default should be to not make any assumptions about `/usr`.

The latest version makes the trust-from-directories mode disabled by default, and it can be opted-in via a meson build option or an env var. While I'd prefer a custom polkit rule instead as you suggested, it's not a strong opinion and I'm fine either way.

issue_context.title: rootless systemd-nspawn
issue_context.body:
### Component

machinectl, systemd-nspawn

### Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe

As mentioned [here](https://github.com/systemd/mkosi/issues/726#issuecomment-863028220) by @poettering, a rootless mode for systemd-nspawn would be great to be able to boot into a container without needing root. As that comment was a few years ago and I didn't find an open feature request I'd like to just open this one to revive that idea and ask nicely about the progress on it.


### Describe the solution you'd like

on Jun 17, 2021 @poettering described it as:
> systemd-nspawn does not support invocation by non-root users though, but that#s something to address in nspawn

Basically I'd like to be able to use systemd-nspawn to start a container without the invoking user having to have root privileges to allow for a rootless usage. Usages are for example within "makechrootpkg" on archlinux (which uses systemd-nspawn internally) to run reproducible builds without needing needing root privileges to enter the build environment.

### Describe alternatives you've considered

A yanked setup using a combination of unshare, chroot, and bind mounts to launch nspawn within a separate namespace without root privileges. I've seen it being mentioned in some docs for non-systemd systems, but the instructions weren't entirely clear and complete, so I didn't try if that actually works. But systemd these days sometimes also runs within docker containers, so it probably will.
While testing my main issue was to mount /dev into the new root directory, but anything else appeared to just work. Sadly because of the problems with /dev systemd couldn't be initialized within the new namespace and just failed to start with a permission error.

### The systemd version you checked that didn't have the feature you are asking for

254

Currently the nspawn documentation states for its `--user` flag, which is different from systemd.exec's `User=`:

> Like all other systemd-nspawn features, this is not a security feature [...]

My guess would be that using `User=dynamic` and rootless nspawn might improve security compared to the status quo?
